title: Accusative case
blurb: The case for direct objects — what you see, want, buy, or eat directly.

vocab.example: Mám rád fotbal, ale ne hokej.
V obchodě kupuju mléko a chleba.
Znám tvou sestru, chodíme spolu do práce.

grammarNote.title: The direct object changes — but not always the same way
grammarNote.text: The accusative marks the direct object (what you have, see, read, buy...). The ending you change depends on the noun's gender: feminine nouns ending in -a swap it for -u (kniha → knihu, sestra → sestru). Masculine animate nouns (people, animals) usually add -a (pes → psa, bratr → bratra). Masculine inanimate nouns and neuter nouns don't change at all from the nominative (fotbal stays fotbal, mléko stays mléko). Feminine nouns ending in a consonant (like pomoc) also stay the same. So the two safe rules to memorize first: feminine -a → -u, and 'if it's not animate and not feminine -a, it probably doesn't change.'

check.prompt: Which sentence correctly says "I see a dog" (pes → accusative)?
check.explanation: Pes is masculine animate, so the accusative adds -a: psa.
check.note: This -a ending for masculine animate nouns is the same ending you'll see later in the genitive case too.

check.prompt: Neuter nouns change their ending in the accusative case.
check.explanation: Neuter nouns (like mléko) keep the same form in the accusative as in the nominative.
check.note: This makes neuter nouns the easiest gender to handle in the accusative — one less thing to change.

check.prompt: Čtu ___. (kniha, fill in the accusative form)
check.explanation: Kniha is feminine ending in -a, so the accusative swaps -a for -u: knihu.

check.prompt: "kniha" (book) is feminine and takes -u in the accusative: knihu. Give the accusative form of "sestra" (sister): ___
check.explanation: Sestra follows the same feminine -a → -u pattern as kniha, giving sestru.

title: Genitive case
blurb: The case for possession ("of"), quantities ("a lot of", "a little"), and prepositions like bez, od, and z.

vocab.translation: What time is it? (lit. how many of the hours)

grammarNote.title: Genitive: "of", quantities, and a fixed set of prepositions
grammarNote.text: The genitive shows up in three everyday situations. First, possession — "the house of my brother" (dům mého bratra) instead of an apostrophe-s. Second, after quantity words: hodně (a lot of), málo (a little of), kolik (how many/much of), and after numbers five and up (pět korun, deset minut) — the thing being counted goes into the genitive. Third, after a fixed group of common prepositions that always take genitive regardless of meaning: bez (without), od (from), do (into/until), z/ze (out of/from), and u (at/near). There's no shortcut for the endings themselves — feminine -a nouns take -y (voda → vody), most masculine nouns take -a or -u depending on the individual word (bratr → bratra, čas → času) — so for now, focus on recognizing when genitive is required and learn each noun's genitive form as you meet it.

check.prompt: How do you say "a glass of water" in Czech?
check.explanation: Voda is feminine; after the quantity word sklenice, it takes the genitive ending -y: vody.
check.note: This same pattern applies to any "container/amount of X" phrase: kousek chleba, láhev vína, kilo jablek.

check.prompt: The preposition "bez" (without) is always followed by the genitive case.
check.explanation: Bez always takes the genitive, no matter what follows it — bez cukru, bez peněz, bez tebe.
check.note: A handful of prepositions (bez, od, do, z/ze, u) always take genitive — worth memorizing as a fixed list.

check.explanation: Z always takes the genitive, and Praha (feminine -a) becomes Prahy.

check.prompt: "čas" (time) takes -u in the genitive after málo: málo času. Give the genitive form of "cukr" (sugar) after bez: bez ___
check.explanation: Cukr is a masculine noun that also takes -u in the genitive: cukru.

title: Past tense
blurb: Talk about what already happened — the l-participle and how it agrees with who's speaking.

vocab.example: Ahoj, co jsi dělal včera večer?
Včera jsem byla celý den doma.
Ráno jsem šla do práce pěšky.
V poledne jsem jedl oběd v restauraci.
Bohužel jsme přišli pozdě na schůzku.
Počasí bylo hezké, měli jsme štěstí.

grammarNote.title: The l-participle + jsem/jsi — and why the 3rd person drops it
grammarNote.text: Czech forms the past tense with two parts: an l-participle (infinitive stem + -l/-la/-lo/-li/-ly) that agrees with the subject's gender and number, plus the present tense of být as an auxiliary — but only for 1st and 2nd person (já jsem dělal, ty jsi dělal, my jsme dělali, vy jste dělali). The 3rd person (on/ona/ono/oni/ony) drops the auxiliary entirely — just "dělal", "dělala", "dělali" on their own. The l-participle endings: -l (masculine singular), -la (feminine singular), -lo (neuter singular), -li (masculine animate plural), -ly (feminine plural and masculine inanimate plural). One common irregular you'll use constantly: jít (to go) has the irregular past stem šel/šla/šlo/šli/šly instead of a regular -l ending. Also note word order: jsem/jsi are unstressed words that jump to the second position in the sentence, not necessarily right next to the subject — "Včera jsem byl v práci", not "Já včera jsem byl...".

check.prompt: How does a woman say "I went" (jít, past tense)?
check.explanation: Jít has an irregular past stem; the feminine singular form is šla, so a woman says šla jsem.
check.note: Jít is one of the most common irregular l-participles — worth memorizing on its own: šel/šla/šlo/šli/šly.

check.prompt: In the 3rd person (on/ona/ono/oni/ony), Czech past tense uses an auxiliary verb like "jsem".
check.explanation: The 3rd person drops the auxiliary entirely — you just use the l-participle alone: on dělal, ona dělala, oni dělali.
check.note: This trips up a lot of learners going the other way too — don't add jsem/jsi when talking about someone else.

check.prompt: Ona ___ film včera. (vidět, past tense, feminine singular)
check.explanation: Vidět's l-participle is viděl/viděla/vidělo; feminine singular is viděla, and no auxiliary is needed in the 3rd person.

check.prompt: "dělal" is the masculine singular past tense of dělat. Give the feminine plural form (used for "they" when referring to women or things): ___
check.explanation: Feminine plural (and masculine inanimate plural) takes the -ly ending: dělaly.
